subtopics.title: Solving Like an Equation — With One Exception

questions.question: Solving 5x − 2 ≤ 13 gives:
options: x ≤ 3, with the sign unchanged since we divided by a positive

questions.question: The ONE operation that reverses an inequality sign is:
options: Adding a negative number to both sides
Multiplying or dividing both sides by a NEGATIVE number
Subtracting the same quantity from both sides
Dividing both sides by a large positive number

questions.question: Solving −3x > 12 correctly gives:
options: x < −4, because dividing by −3 flips the sign

questions.question: How does testing x = 0 expose the WRONG answer 'x > −4' for −3x > 12?
options: Zero is not allowed in inequalities
x = 0 fits the claimed answer, but −3(0) = 0 is NOT greater than 12 — the claim fails its own inequality

subtopics.title: The Number Line and Interval Notation

questions.question: A SOLID dot on a number-line sketch means:
options: The boundary is included — the sign carries the bar (≤ or ≥)

questions.question: In interval notation, x ≤ 3 is written as:
options: (−∞ ; 3] — round at infinity, square at the included 3

questions.question: Why does infinity ALWAYS take a round bracket?
options: Infinity can never be reached, so it can never be included as an endpoint
Square brackets are reserved for zero

questions.question: If the question restricts x to INTEGERS with x ≤ 3, the number-line answer becomes:
options: Separate dots at 3, 2, 1, 0, −1, ... — no continuous shading

subtopics.title: Compound Inequalities — Trapped Between Two Fences

questions.question: The golden rule for solving −5 ≤ 3x + 1 < 10 is:
options: Perform every operation on all THREE parts simultaneously
Solve the left half first, then guess the right
Work only with the outer numbers

questions.question: The solution of −5 ≤ 3x + 1 < 10 is:
options: −2 ≤ x < 3 — minus two included, three excluded

questions.question: On the number line, −2 ≤ x < 3 is drawn as:
options: A solid dot at −2, a hollow dot at 3, and shading only between them — no arrows
A solid dot at 3 with shading to the right

questions.question: If a compound inequality is divided through by a NEGATIVE number:
options: BOTH signs reverse, and the statement is rewritten with the smaller value on the left

subtopics.title: Word Problems, Integers, and the Trap Museum

questions.question: The stallholder pays R150 for her stand and sells vetkoek at R15 each. 'Profit of at least R450' translates to:
The solution n ≥ 40 is checked at the boundary by:
options: 40 × 15 = 600, minus the R150 fee, leaves exactly R450 — 'at least' is satisfied by 40 itself

questions.question: Which phrase means STRICTLY greater than?
The trap-museum exhibit called the 'phantom flip' is:
options: Flipping the sign twice when dividing by a negative
Shading both sides of the boundary
Reversing the sign merely because a negative number was ADDED or subtracted — where no flip belongs

questions.question: R400 beats R250 in your pocket, but owing R400 is worse than owing R250. This explains why:
options: Multiplying both sides of an inequality by a negative must flip the sign — amounts dragged into debt reverse their order

questions.question: In symbols, the debt picture says:
The ten-second defence against flip errors is:
options: Testing one value from your answer in the ORIGINAL inequality — it must satisfy it

questions.question: 'Sixteen and older admitted' versus 'older than sixteen': the sixteen-year-old at the gate:
options: Walks in under the first sign but stays outside under the second — the boundary's fate hangs on one word
Must wait a year either way

questions.question: In interval notation, the square bracket plays the same role as:
options: The filled dot — the boundary is admitted

questions.question: The ordering rule for writing an interval is:
options: The smaller number stands first, matching the number line's own direction

subtopics.title: Between Two Fences, and the Vetkoek Test

questions.question: 'At least fourteen but under nineteen' puts the two gates at:
Solving −5 ≤ 3x + 1 < 10 'like serving all three plates together' means:
options: Working left to right one part at a time
Subtracting 1 from all three parts, then dividing all three by 3, landing on −2 ≤ x < 3

questions.question: Why is the dot at n = 40 filled in the vetkoek answer?
options: Because dots at multiples of ten are always filled
Because the shading needs an endpoint
Because the fortieth vetkoek lands the profit at exactly R450, and 'at least' includes hitting the target exactly

questions.question: The full-marks final line of a context question speaks:
options: The story's language — 'she must sell at least forty vetkoek', not just 'n ≥ 40'
